title: Footprints on the Moon
sub: PreK–Kindergarten · Apollo 11 and the Moon’s dust
objective: Children will hear that, in 1969, astronauts flew to the Moon and walked on it, and that twelve astronauts have walked there in all. They will see for themselves that wind and rain wipe a footprint away, and learn that the Moon has no wind or rain, so the astronauts’ footprints are still there. They will use describing words for Moon dust: sharp, sticky, and smelling like gunpowder.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: The Moon is a real place, and people have walked there. Footprints show how different it is from home.

materials: A shallow tray of flour or fine sand, smoothed flat, and a shoe or boot to press into it
A small spray bottle of water, or a cup to sprinkle from
The *Show your class* page (page 3), projected or printed
questions: Who walked on the Moon? How many astronauts went, and how many walked?
What happened to our footprint when the wind blew and the rain fell?
Why are the astronauts’ footprints still on the Moon?
If you walked on the Moon, what would you want to see?
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** on the poster *Our Incredible Moon,* find the big Moon and the panel *“The Eagle has landed.”* Listen for the recording as the panel arrives.
**Virtual visit:** in *Under the Microscope,* wipe a slide and put real Moon dust on it. Watch how it clings to the cloth.

steps.title: A mystery in the tray
script: Before the children arrive, press a shoe firmly into the tray so it leaves a clear print. Sit in a circle around it. Ask: *“Who made this footprint? How could we make it go away?”* Let them guess and point to the ridges of the sole. Then: *“Today we will hear about footprints in a very faraway place. They have been there for a long, long time.”*

screen.question: Who made this footprint? How could we make it go away?

steps.purpose: Wonder about a footprint before hearing whose footprints are on the Moon.
students: Look at the footprint in the tray.

steps.title: Our Moon
script: Show the Moon on the screen or page 3. *“This is our Moon, the one we see at night. A long time ago, in 1969, three astronauts flew all the way there in a rocket.”* Two of them, **Neil Armstrong** and **Buzz Aldrin**, landed their little spacecraft, called the *Eagle*, and walked on the Moon. The third, **Michael Collins**, flew round and round the Moon, waiting for them.

screen.caption: Our Incredible Moon
screen.alt: A huge lavender Moon rising, with gray patches and round craters on its face

steps.purpose: Look at the Moon, and hear that people have been there.
students: What can you see on the Moon?

steps.title: The Eagle has landed
script: Play the recording: these are the real words sent back to Earth when the *Eagle* landed. Count together: *three* astronauts went, *two* walked on the Moon. Since then, **twelve** astronauts have walked on the Moon. The Moon’s dust was very fine, sharp and sticky: it stuck to everything, and the astronauts said it smelled like gunpowder.

clips.label: “The Eagle has landed”
clips.credit: Apollo 11 air-to-ground audio, NASA · “The Eagle Has Landed,” freesound_community, Pixabay

screen.question: This was really said on the Moon. What do you hear?

steps.purpose: Hear a real recording from the day astronauts first landed on the Moon.
students: How many astronauts went? How many walked on the Moon?

steps.title: Try it
script: Let two or three children blow gently across the tray, like the wind. Let another sprinkle a little water, like the rain. *“What is happening to our footprint?”* The edges soften and blur. On Earth, wind and rain wipe footprints away.

screen.question: Blow like the wind. Sprinkle like the rain. What happens to the footprint?

steps.purpose: See for themselves what wind and rain do to a footprint on Earth.

steps.title: Still there
script: *“But the Moon has no wind. The Moon has no rain.”* Read the words on the screen: The Moon has no wind or rain, so the astronauts’ footprints will probably last for millions of years. *“So the astronauts’ footprints are still there today.”*

screen.text: The Moon has no wind or rain, so the astronauts’ footprints will probably last for millions of years.

steps.purpose: Learn why the astronauts’ footprints are still on the Moon.

steps.title: Your handout
script: Each child works on a handout. All three show the same footprints, the same wind and rain, and the same Moon.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Picture-led. Count the footprints and circle the number, color the wind and the rain, trace *MOON*, then draw a footprint on the Moon.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: A little writing. Count the footprints, draw lines to show where a footprint stays and where it is wiped away, copy *MOON* under a model, then draw an astronaut’s footprints.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Draw and tell. Match Earth and the Moon to what happens to a footprint, circle the words for Moon dust and tell a grown-up why, then finish the sentence *On the Moon, my footprint would…*

steps.purpose: Count, match and draw on paper, at the right level for each child.
students: Why do footprints stay on the Moon? Find it on your page.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the questions on the screen. For each one, the children show a thumb up, sideways or down: *“Can you now say who walked on the Moon? Can you now say why footprints stay on the Moon? Can you now tell what Moon dust is like?”*

screen.hint: Show me: thumb up, sideways or down.

steps.purpose: Check what each child can now do against the objectives.
students: say who walked on the Moon?
say why footprints stay on the Moon?
tell what Moon dust is like?

steps.title: One small step
script: Stand up together. Tell the children what Neil Armstrong said when he stepped onto the Moon: *“That’s one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind.”* Everyone takes one small step on the spot, then one giant leap.

screen.text: That’s one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind.

steps.purpose: Close with Neil Armstrong’s words, and a step and a leap of their own.
